newsitem.title: UK: Britain holds off deciding on BA/American.
newsitem.headline: Britain holds off deciding on BA/American.

text.p: Britain is believed to have put off its long awaited ruling on the proposed alliance between British Airways and American Airlines until mid-November, airline industry sources said on Wednesday.

The industry has been waiting for trade minister Ian Lang to decide whether or not to block the deal ever since his Office of Fair Trading (OFT) completed an investigation into the competition issues on September 17.
But Lang is believed to have stepped back from making a decision to make way for a new round of "open skies" aviation trade talks between Britain and the United States.
These talks are to be held in Washington next week.
However, they said there was still no indication that the two governments can reach agreement for open skies, which would smooth the way for Lang to approve the BA and American alliance.
Britain said earlier today that the talks aimed at liberalising the Anglo-U.S. air travel market are to resume on November 6, at the request of U.S. negotiators.
"This is a surprising twist in that the talks are back on again but I still think there is a long way to go," said an executive with a U.S. airline.
The U.S. Department of Transportation broke off the last round of talks, due in August, because of the lack of progress made in the opening sessions.

Washington has made any approval of the BA/American alliance conditional on getting open skies with Britain, and in particular in getting open access for all U.S. carriers to London's Heathrow, Europe's most popular airport.

But rival U.S. and British carriers say Heathrow is so overcrowded that open access would be meaningless unless they were to be granted some of British Airways' 38 percent share of existing takeoff and landing slots.

Industry sources said if next week's talks in Washington go well a second round of talks in London has been pencilled in by negotiators and airline lobbyists for the week of November 18, the same week in which Lang is now expected to make his ruling.

The fresh attempt at agreeing an "open skies" deal began in July after British Airways and American urged the governments to free up competition as a necessary condition for approving their plans to join forces on the transatlantic market.

Airline industry sources said on Wednesday that they believed next week's meeting was designed by both sides to thrash out a compromise deal since airline representatives have been told they are to be excluded from the session.
Normally British and U.S. airlines are allowed to send representatives to the meetings to promote their interests.
"The meeting will not include airlines but it is a formal meeting between sets of officials from the two governments," said one industry source.

Meanwhile there is also speculation that Lang is still trying to reconcile the conflicting arguments for and against allowing the BA/American alliance to go through without a full investigation by the UK Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
Lang is seen most likely to give the alliance qualified clearance, provided that BA's home hub of London Heathrow is opened up to competition.
But opponents such as British long haul operator Virgin Atlantic hope he will impose such onerous conditions that the deal won't be able to get off the ground.
